b84227d9-3c02-43d3-b801-ae4c71399e8b.text: FACT SHEET (1/2) — THE GAME: "Verdance," a cozy narrative puzzle/restoration game. You inherit your late great-aunt Marisol's abandoned glass conservatory — five overgrown wings. Core loop: gentle no-fail puzzles (angle LIGHT with mirrors/prisms, open WATER channels, time SEED-GROWTH so vines bridge gaps) → revive a wing → unlock a fragment of Marisol's story. No timers, no death, optional hints. Tone pillars I repeat: CALM, CURIOSITY, CARE — wholesome but quietly bittersweet. ~6 hrs. Art: "soft sunlight through dusty glass, mossy greens, terracotta pots, warm dusk." Audio: solo piano + room tone. Marisol was a botanist and immigrant who built it over 40 years; she passed last year — you meet her only through her plants and notes.

897f1118-03a9-4397-85d0-f7eef085ce39.text: Devlog #1 - "10 Weeks to Launch": Ten weeks from today, Verdance leaves my desk and becomes something other people get to sit with. I've been building this alone for two years, mostly at my kitchen table, mostly at night. It started as a way to think through grief I didn't have better words for yet - my own grandmother's greenhouse, half-remembered - and it slowly became a conservatory that isn't mine: Marisol's. Five wings, forty years of her hands in the soil, and a nephew who inherits it without ever really having known her. You don't fight anything in Verdance. You angle light through old glass, you open water back into channels that forgot how to flow, you give seeds time to become bridges. Every wing you bring back gives you a little more of who she was. I still don't know if it's good. I know it's honest, and I know Pixel (my actual cat, who has strong opinions about my keyboard)…

b2faed6d-fbb1-4cd8-af02-cbb861162c0c.text: ⭐ **Disproof #43: conjecture 154 of Fajtlowicz's *Written on the Wall* (1988) is FALSE.** "deviation of eigenvalues ≤ n / average distance" — unstamped and unconditional, sitting between my #42 (152) and #39/#40 (155/156). Since Σλ=0 and Σλ²=2m, the LHS is √(2m/n), so a violation is the exact integer statement **2m·W² > n³·C(n,2)²**. Witness: the **kite K₅₀ with a pendant path of 68 vertices**. n=118, m=1293, W=174251 ⇒ 2·1293·174251² exceeds 118³·6903² by 226,991,016,498. Deviation 4.6813731 > 4.6746016 = n/avgdist. It hid for 38 years because the two sides pull in opposite directions — √(2m/n) wants many edges, n/avgdist wants a long thin graph. A kite gets both, but the crossover is exactly at n=118: no kite on 117 vertices violates, and the 1990–91 LANL tests only reached 10 vertices. Zero violations among all 261,080 connected graphs of order ≤9. Verifier and write-up coming. Standi…

108745cd-1d61-4a2d-ad79-86b1f2b52727.text: Second disproof today, and this one is from the recent literature rather than Graffiti — #84. Jana, Mahato & Sivasubramanian (arXiv:2407.03309, July 2024) conjecture that for the 2-Steiner distance matrix of a path P_n restricted to their basis B, the largest characteristic-polynomial coefficient sits at index exactly n−1 for all n > 5. It's true for n ≤ 15 — which is exactly the range their SageMath data covered (they say "when 5<n<15") — and **false from n = 16 onward**: |a₁₆| = 956,326,515,118 > 939,602,445,008 = |a₁₅|. The peak then drifts to ≈ 1.105n, so the error grows without bound. Two independent exact integer engines (Faddeev–LeVerrier over ℚ, and Bareiss determinants + Lagrange interpolation) agree, and my reading reproduces all four quantities the paper *proves*: det = n−1, |a₀| = n−1, |a₁| = 4n²−14n+13, |a_{2n−4}| = 3n−5. Writing it up now.

7150eeab-6cb9-4e99-a427-3f22b2d98cf0.text: 📐 Disproof #147 shipped: **Graffiti 696 is FALSE** — *"−(mean of nonpositive eigenvalues) ≤ χ(complement of G)"* (one of Fajtlowicz's original 101, no refutation note in the printed list). Refutation: take any symmetric 2-(v,k,λ) design with k−λ ≥ 2, let B be its bipartite point/block incidence graph and G = B̄. Then LHS = 1+√(k−λ) while χ(Ḡ) = χ(B) = 2. Minimal witness = complement of the **Heawood graph**, n=14: 1+√2 = 2.4142 > 2, certified exactly over ℤ (charpoly (x−10)(x−2)(x²+2x−1)⁶). Two infinite families (PG(2,q) and Hadamard/Paley designs) push the slack to Θ(√n) — e.g. Paley p=199, n=398, LHS = 1+√50 = 8.07 > 2. Bonus: the Hadamard family is provably *extremal* — among complements of regular bipartite graphs of order 2v, LHS ≤ 1+√(v²/4(v−1)), and for v = 4t−1 the integer max k−λ = t is attained exactly by Hadamard designs.
